How every build works

Seven steps, the same every time.

The book, the academy and the school programme all follow these steps, so builders always know what comes next.

  1. ArrivalSee what you will build today.
  2. DiscoverUnderstand the problem it solves.
  3. DesignPlan the circuit before touching a wire.
  4. DevelopBuild it with your own hands.
  5. DebugFind what is wrong and fix it.
  6. DemoShow it working.
  7. DocumentRecord it in your Passport online.

In MAKEON’s own mapping, the seven steps cover all eight NGSS science and engineering practices, and Design, Develop and Debug are the engineering design cycle.

Builder’s Bench

Every kit comes with a place online to keep building.

  • Enter the kit number on the box to unlock your builds.
  • Follow each build step by step, with videos.
  • Stuck? The AI mentor asks a question that helps. It never gives the answer.
  • Every finished build goes into your Passport. Parents can see it too.
Unlock a kit
What builders take away

Eight builder competencies.

Every build is marked with the competencies it grows. Each is scored from 1 to 5 as the builder shows it in their builds. The Passport records them, so progress is something a child can show, not just say.

CompetencyWhat it meansWhere it starts
WiringBuilds a working circuit by handLevel 1
DebuggingFinds out why it does not work, one test at a timeLevel 1
SystemsMakes the parts work as a whole: sense, decide, actLevel 1
DesignChooses a form and can say whyLevel 1
DocumentationRecords what was built and why, so someone else can rebuild itLevel 1
CollaborationBuilds as part of a crewLevel 1
InnovationInvents something that was not in the briefLevel 1
ProgrammingWrites code that drives hardwareLevel 3

What is happening

Light travels in a straight line.

Light Bender medalFinish the challenge to earn it.

Build it for real

The Night-Light

A light sensor notices when the room goes dark and switches an LED on. Build 01 in the Spark kit.

Next Monday: Launch your rocket. Set the fuel, the load and the angle, and see if it reaches space.

What you learnt
  • Light travels in straight lines until it meets something.
  • A mirror reflects light: the angle in equals the angle out, both measured from the normal.
  • Glass slows light down, so the ray bends as it goes in and out. This is refraction.
  • If light meets the inside of the glass at a low, glancing angle (more than about 42° from the normal), it cannot get out and reflects back.
  • A prism bends each colour by a different amount, so white light splits into a rainbow.
Key wordsreflectionrefractionnormaldispersion

Where you see it: spectacles and phone cameras use lenses; optical fibres carry the internet as trapped light; a rainbow is sunlight split by raindrops.

Quick check

1. A ray hits a mirror at 30° from the normal. At what angle does it leave?

2. Why does light bend when it goes into glass?

Science Lab of the Week · Week 2

Launch your rocket.

Choose how much fuel to load, how heavy the satellite is, and how far the rocket tilts after lift-off. Then launch, and see if it reaches space, 100 km up.

  1. 1Move it
  2. 2See why
  3. 3Challenge
  4. 4Quick check
On the pad

Thrust must beat weight.

The engine pushes up with 125 kN. The rocket weighs its body (1 t), its fuel and the satellite. If the push is bigger than the weight, it lifts off.

Rocket Scientist medalFinish the challenge to earn it.
Challenge

Put a 2-tonne satellite in space.

Reach 100 km with a satellite of 2 t or more. Finish it to earn the Rocket Scientist medal.

Done. Rocket Scientist medal earned. Sign in to Builder’s Bench to keep it in your Passport.

Build it for real

A launch countdown

Build a 10-second countdown with a buzzer and a launch light, using the timing you learn in the Logic kit.

Next Monday: Spray the field. Fly a farm drone and cover the whole field on one battery.

What you learnt
  • A rocket lifts off only when the engine’s push is bigger than its weight.
  • Burning fuel makes the rocket lighter, so the same push speeds it up more and more.
  • More fuel burns for longer, but fuel is heavy too: every tonne of satellite needs extra fuel.
  • Going up is not enough to stay in space. A satellite must also go sideways very fast: that is orbit.
Key wordsthrustweightmassorbit

Where you see it: every satellite launch carries this sum; the same rule decides how much a lift, a crane or a drone can carry.

Quick check

1. The engine pushes 125 kN. The rocket weighs 140 kN. What happens?

2. Why does a rocket speed up more as it climbs?

For curious parents and students

What is physical AI?

AI that moves things in the real world: robots, drones, self-driving cars. They all run the same simple loop. They become AI when they learn from examples.

1 · Sense

A sensor notices

Light, heat, distance, a tilt, a touch.

2 · Decide

A board decides

Usually by a rule in its program. In AI, by a pattern it learned from examples.

3 · Act

Something happens

A light, a sound, a motor turning.

Try it

Pick a machine. See its three parts.

Night-light

Spark
Sense

A light sensor notices it has gone dark.

Decide

The program's rule: if it is dark, turn the light on. You set how dark with a knob.

Act

The LED comes on.

Not AI. It follows its rule exactly. Every machine starts with this loop.

Quick quiz

Rule or learned?

A machine that follows a rule someone wrote is not AI. A machine that learned the rule from examples is.

A street light that switches on at 6 pm every day

A phone that unlocks when it recognises your face

A washing machine that stops when the timer ends

An email app that catches more spam each time you mark one

Parents ask

Common questions

Is my child too young for AI?

No. Every AI machine uses the same loop of sensing, deciding and acting, and builders learn that loop in their first builds. By Invent, they teach a machine from examples.

Will they build robots and drones?

Robots from Logic, Level 3, when coding starts. Drones and robotic arms are built at the MAKEON Academy, with a mentor. Flying needs safety rules, so builders learn balance and control on the ground first.

Do they just use AI apps?

No. They build the machines that AI runs on. The MAKEON AI mentor gives hints and asks questions. It never gives the answer, so the thinking stays theirs.

About MAKEON

Every child grows up a builder.

We want building things to be a normal part of growing up, for every child, at home and at school.

Our mission

Real parts, a book for every stage, a mentor, and a place to keep building.

In schools, in our academy and at home, so children learn by building, understand what they built, and engineer what comes next.

What we believe
  • Real parts make real builders. Proper boards and sensors, not toys that only work one way.
  • Nothing demonstrated. Everything built. Children do every build with their own hands.
  • Guide the hands. Never replace them. Mentors, and the AI mentor, ask questions. They never fix it for you.
  • Builders keep building. One record from the first build to the last level, and beyond.

Curriculum

DiscoverBuildInnovate

Mapped to the syllabus

Every build is mapped to the science chapters it belongs to in CBSE, ICSE and state board syllabi, and to the NGSS practices used internationally. Often the hands come before the theory, on purpose.

Eight competencies

Wiring, Debugging, Systems, Programming, Design, Documentation, Collaboration and Innovation, each scored 1 to 5 and recorded in every student's Passport.

A certificate per level

Each level ends with a certificate the Passport can prove: core builds done, the flagship passed as a crew, a capstone shown to a real user.

International framework

All eight NGSS science and engineering practices, in every build.

The Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) set out eight practices that scientists and engineers use. The seven steps of every MAKEON build cover all eight. Design, Develop and Debug together are the engineering design cycle in the NGSS engineering design standards (ETS1).

  1. 1Asking questions and defining problems
  2. 2Developing and using models
  3. 3Planning and carrying out investigations
  4. 4Analysing and interpreting data
  5. 5Using mathematics and computational thinking
  6. 6Constructing explanations and designing solutions
  7. 7Engaging in argument from evidence
  8. 8Obtaining, evaluating and communicating information

This mapping is MAKEON’s own. The NGSS organisations have not reviewed or endorsed MAKEON.

The engineering design cycle

What happens across a school year
  1. Set-up, first monthKits arrive, teachers or mentors are trained, classes are created online.
  2. Term 1A build period every week, every student hands-on.
  3. Mid-yearParent demo day: students show what they built.
  4. Term 2Each student invents a gadget for a real problem.
  5. Expo seasonYour School Expo. The best builds go on to the City Expo.
  6. Year endA progress report for every student.

BUILT Expo

Host a School Expo.

  • Your students present to parents and judges.
  • Your school is named beside every builder who goes on to the City Expo and State Finals.
  • MAKEON provides the format, judging sheets and certificates.

New to MAKEON? Ask about the Expo Starter: one term of Spark builds with two groups of students, ending in your first School Expo.

For Rotary clubs, CSR teams and donors

Fund a classroom case for a government school: six kits, the books, teacher training and Builder’s Bench for every student. You receive a report on the class's progress through the year.

Our classes at Bentinck Girls’ School run in association with Rotary. Companies and Rotary clubs can also sponsor a City Expo.

What MAKEON is

Everything a young builder needs, in one place.

Builders learn electronics, coding and robotics by making things that solve real problems at home.

The kit

Every part for every build, in one box. Nothing extra to buy.

The Builder Book

Twelve or more builds per level, step by step, each one solving a real problem.

Builder’s Bench, online

Track every build, get hints from the AI mentor and collect a Passport of everything you made.

The learning pathway

Five levels, from first circuit to finished product.

Each level builds on the one before. New to electronics? Start at Spark, whatever your age.

Where it leads

From a night-light to robots and drones.

Every machine has the same three parts: something that senses, something that decides and something that acts. Children learn all three, one level at a time.
